title: Enhancing vocational students’ professional competencies through AI agent-supported human–AI collaborative learning: A longitudinal mixed-methods study
extended_summary:
The paper addresses the challenge of providing authentic, interactive, competency-oriented vocational training in cross-border e-commerce. Traditional case-based instruction and static simulations are described as insufficient for giving students repeated practice, continuous feedback, and realistic exposure to customer-management scenarios such as logistics disputes, customer complaints, and social media crises. The study asks how a structured human–AI collaborative teaching system affects perceived instructional quality over time, how students use and perceive role-specialized AI agents, and what strengths and limitations students identify in a triadic student–instructor–AI model.

The intervention is an AI agent-based collaborative teaching system built around multiple large-language-model-powered agents. These include an AI Customer Agent for simulated customer interactions, an AI Data Analyst Agent for decision support using logistics and customer data, and an AI Mentor Agent for procedural guidance based on cross-border e-commerce SOPs and policies. The instructional model uses pre-class AI-assisted practice, in-class human–AI collaborative simulation and instructor-led debriefing, and post-class reflection and system refinement. The system also uses retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering, short-term dialogue memory, and data logging to support iterative improvement.

The study was conducted in a mandatory “Cross-Border E-Commerce Customer Management” course at Shenzhen Polytechnic University in China. Participants were vocational students enrolled across four academic years from 2022 to 2025, with longitudinal teaching evaluation data from 232 students, quantitative survey responses from 117 students, and qualitative reflection data from 35 students. Instructors were also part of the pedagogical model, serving as scenario designers, facilitators, and strategic mentors, though student data formed the main empirical basis.

The study reports that average student teaching evaluation scores increased from 90.58 in the pre-AI year of 2022 to 93.81 in 2025, with the largest gain occurring after the initial AI implementation. Students strongly preferred AI simulation training over traditional lectures and valued the realism, immediacy, and decision-support functions of the AI agents. The authors conclude that structured role-specialized AI agents can shift generative AI from a general-purpose tool to a collaborative educational partner in vocational education, while noting limitations such as lack of emotional intelligence, mechanical responses, single-site implementation, and reliance on subjective evaluation measures.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: An unnamed LLM-powered multi-agent educational system using role-specialized AI agents for simulated dialogue, decision support, and instructional guidance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in a vocational Cross-Border E-Commerce Customer Management course as role-specialized AI agents: an AI Customer Agent for simulated customer conversations, an AI Data Analyst Agent for logistics/customer-value decision support, and an AI Mentor Agent for procedural guidance and SOP-based feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Across four cohorts in a mandatory Cross-Border E-Commerce Customer Management course, official student evaluation of teaching scores increased from 90.58 in the pre-AI year 2022 (n=57) to 93.37 in 2023 (n=62), 93.73 in 2024 (n=63), and 93.81 in 2025 (n=50), for total N=232. The largest reported gain was +2.79 points from 2022 to 2023, coinciding with the initial transition to the AI Simulation + Teacher Collaboration model.
findings.measure: Official student evaluation of teaching scores / perceived instructional quality

findings.finding_summary: In the AI Agent Simulation Training Feedback survey, 81.2% of students identified AI Simulation Training as their preferred pedagogical approach, compared with 26.5% identifying traditional theoretical lectures. The study reports this as evidence of student endorsement and pedagogical acceptance of the human-AI collaborative training model.
findings.measure: Student pedagogical method preference / endorsement survey

findings.finding_summary: Perceived interaction realism had a high descriptive mean score of 4.03 (SD=0.67). Pearson correlation analysis showed a significant positive relationship between perceived interaction realism and overall acceptance of the human-AI collaborative model, r=0.621, p<0.01, N=117, with approximately 38.6% of variance in acceptance associated with perceived realism.
findings.measure: Perceived interaction realism and acceptance of the human-AI collaborative model

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative reflections were generally positive about AI agents as efficient practice partners and immediate resource repositories, but approximately 45% of reflections reported that AI responses sometimes felt mechanical or disconnected from context. Students also noted excessive verbosity, formatting errors and special symbols in exported content, and difficulty with complex multi-layered queries requiring multiple prompt adjustments.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal mixed-methods study using convenience samples, institutional teaching evaluations, surveys, and qualitative reflections. The authors describe the design as quasi-experimental but note no randomized or parallel control group, possible cohort effects, and possible novelty effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports positive perceived outcomes, including SET scores increasing from 90.58 to 93.81 and a moderate-to-large correlation between perceived realism and acceptance (r=0.621). However, impacts are based mainly on subjective evaluation, acceptance, and survey measures with no reported standardized causal effect size for learning outcomes.
